ABSTRACT
Medical image segmentation enables doctors to observe lesion regions better and make accurate diagnostic
decisions. Single-branch models such as U-Net have achieved great progress in this field. However, the com-
plementary local and global pathological semantics of heterogeneous neural networks have not yet been fully
explored. The class-imbalance problem remains a serious issue. To alleviate these two problems, we propose a
novel model called BCU-Net, which leverages the advantages of ConvNeXt in global interaction and U-Net in
local processing. We propose a new multilabel recall loss (MRL) module to relieve the class imbalance problem
and facilitate deep-level fusion of local and global pathological semantics between the two heterogeneous
branches. Extensive experiments were conducted on six medical image datasets including retinal vessel and
polyp images. The qualitative and quantitative results demonstrate the superiority and generalizability of BCU-
Net. In particular, BCU-Net can handle diverse medical images with diverse resolutions. It has a flexible structure
owing to its plug-and-play characteristics, which promotes its practicality.

advantages in global relationship modeling. Hence, to mine global in-
formation in medical images, TransUNet [38], TransFuse [39],
PCAT-UNet [40], and UTNet [41] have been designed by combining
Transformer and U-Net in diverse ways. These methods [38–41] have
obtained convincing results. However, they used a transformer model
directly to achieve global relationship modeling, leading to very com-
plex network structures. In addition, the traditional transformer struc-
ture inevitably loses key positional information even with the addition

Researchers typically employ a single-branch model to implement
medical image segmentation in most scenarios. Owing to the natural
characteristics of a single network, it extracts only specific pathological
semantics, such as local or global information. As described above, U-
Net uses small convolutions to extract local information. TransUNet
focuses on the extraction of global information. Two-branch models
have recently attracted increasing attention in computer vision (CV). For
example, Mobile-Former [42], a parallel design of MobileNet and
Transformer with a two-way bridge in between, leverages the advan-
tages of MobileNet for local processing and Transformer for global
extraction. It exhibited superior performance in image classification and
object detection tasks. Similar to Mobile-Former, other researchers have
built two-branch medical image segmentation models, such as W-net
[43], Medical Transformer [44], DoubleU-Net [45], and S-UNet [46].
They intend to create bridges" between different branches and fully
exploit the advantages of each branch. However, most of these studies
used only two homogeneous networks to generate segmentation models.
However, the complementary local and global pathological semantics of
heterogeneous networks have not been fully explored. To this end, we go
beyond the standard U-Net framework and investigate the possibility of
bridging two heterogeneous networks smartly and conveniently to mine
sufficient pathological semantics and complete medical image segmen-
tation more effectively.
To appreciate the capabilities of U-Net, we scrutinized its network
architecture and identified some core areas for model improvement. To
make full use of the global and local pathological semantics in the
medical images, on the one hand, we embed the ConvNeXt [47] into our
two-branch model seamlessly. As we know ConvNeXt, with an encoding
structure, has been successfully used for various CV tasks, including
brain age estimation [48], speech recognition [49], crack detection
[50], and breast malignancy prediction [51]. It absorbs the latest
advanced technologies of transformers into the traditional CNN struc-
ture and explores the inverted bottleneck design and large kernels. On
the other hand, inspired by Mobile-Former [42], W-net [43], and
DoubleU-Net [45], we seamlessly bridge U-Net and ConvNeXt in parallel
to mine the complementary pathological semantics between the two
heterogeneous networks. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first
study that bridges U-Net and ConvNeXt in medical image segmentation.
Finally, we propose a new multilabel recall loss (MRL) module to
address the class imbalance problem. We designed a novel two-branch
model called BCU-Net for medical image segmentation. Here, "B"
means bridge, “C" represents ConvNeXt and “U-Net" represents U-Net.
We validated BCU-Net using six medical image datasets. Extensive ex-
periments show that BCU-Net has a highly competitive performance
compared to the most advanced baselines. This study makes four con-
ceptual and empirical contributions:
1) We redesigned the original ConvNeXt to satisfy the encoder-decoder
structure, which is suitable for medical image segmentation and built
a firm foundation for BCU-Net. To the best of our knowledge, this is
the first study employing ConvNeXt for medical image segmentation.
2) We propose BCU-Net, which seamlessly bridges U-Net and ConvNeXt
using a loss function. BCU-Net not only alleviates the class imbalance
problem but also makes full use of the complementary local and
global pathological semantics between the two heterogeneous
networks.
3) Extensive experiments on six medical image datasets demonstrated
the effectiveness and robustness of BCU-Net. Notably, BCU-Net and
its variants achieved satisfactory segmentation performance. BCU-
Net code is available at https://github.com/ZX-ECJTU/BCU-Net.
4) BCU-Net is plug-and-play and more flexible. This required fewer
network interactions. Each branch of BCU-Net can be replaced with
other off-the-shelf segmentation networks. More importantly, BCU-
Net has two-dimensional generalization capabilities. First, it works
on different datasets, including blood vessel and polyp images. Sec-
ond, it handles medical images of different resolutions well.

review existing related research. In Section 3, we present the detailed
design information of the BCU-Net. The experimental results are pre-
sented in Section 4. The discussion and conclusions are presented in
Section 5.

2.1. Medical image segmentation
With the rapid development of neural networks, encoder-decoder-
based structures such as U-Net [12] have achieved remarkable prog-
ress in the field of medical image segmentation. Inspired by U-Net, an
increasing number of researchers have focused on modifying the
encoder-decoder structure to obtain a more satisfactory segmentation
performance. Therefore, we must first provide a concise review of this
study.
Zhou et al. [52] proposed U-Net++ using a group of nested and
dense skipping connections to aggregate multiscale features. U-Net++
exhibits superior performance for different morphologies, including
polyps, nuclei, liver, and brain tumors. Cui et al. [53] embedded a
spatial pyramid pool into skip connections, which helped to acquire
multiscale features for retinal vessel segmentation. Huang et al. [54]
proposed U-Net3+ optimize full-size features for liver CT segmentation.
Unlike previous works [52–54], Huang et al. [55] and Jha et al. [56]
inserted a squeeze and excitation module into each convolutional layer
to effectively facilitate feature extraction. Rather than modifying the
structure of U-Net, other researchers employed diverse losses, including

U-Net. Each loss type addresses a specific segmentation problem. The
aforementioned methods [52–59] pay more attention to the extraction
of local pathological semantics owing to the use of a small convolution.
Most global information was ignored, which affected the final segmen-
tation performance. To alleviate this problem, numerous multiscale
dilated convolution modules [60–62] providing larger receptive fields
have been proposed to extract sufficient global pathological informa-

contextual path with multiscale convolution blocks, was designed to

2.2. Two-branch segmentation model
Recently, two-branch models have been shown to play an important
role in CV. For example, Mobile-Former [42], a parallel design of
MobileNet and Transformer with a two-way bridge between them, was
proposed to implement image classification and object detection. Tan
et al. [64] proposed a two-branch parallel deep fusion network for 3D
object detection. Neven et al. [65] designed a two-branch network for
pixel-based defect segmentation and severity estimations. Bao et al. [66]
proposed a two-branch deep network for 3D point cloud classification.
Ma et al. [67] combined a multiscale matched filter and a U-net model to
extract vascular features using three channels and fused the segmenta-
tion results of the three channels.
Recently, inspired by the two-branch studies above, researchers
introduced the two-branch idea into medical image segmentation. Chen
et al. [43] utilized a bridging method to connect two U-Nets, making full
use of the complementarity of the two networks to improve the final
performance. Kumar et al. [68] proposed a dual U-Net architecture using
an improved Swish function for brain-tumor segmentation. Zhuang et al.
[69] implemented two U-Net links for retinal vessel segmentation.
Zhuang's model contains multiple encoder-decoder branches and allows
for more information flow. Huang et al. [70] designed a two-branch
U-Net model that allowed one branch to be trained using weighting
schemes, emphasizing harder examples to improve the overall seg-
mentation performance.
In summary, these two-branch methods [43,68–70] added too many
skip connections between the two networks. This increases the
complexity of the corresponding model and reduces its practicality. Each
branch of these models focuses on the extraction of local pathological
semantics. This significant global information, which is useful for
medical image segmentation, is partly ignored. Third, the class imbal-
ance problem remains a serious problem in current methods. Finally,
most of these studies tended to use homogeneous rather than hetero-
geneous networks to create two-branch segmentation models. The im-
plicit pathological correlations between heterogeneous branches are not
fully mined, which helps boost the final segmentation performance.
These problems inspired us to design a novel two-branch segmentation
model using two heterogeneous but complementary neural networks.
The new model should make the best of all types of pathological se-
mantics and address the class-imbalance problem. However, it does not
require additional parameters, which improves its practicality. Table 1

3. BCU-Net
Problem definition: The medical image segmentation task in this
study is a type of binary classification task. Each segmented image
contains two types of samples, including foreground objects (we usually
use “1" to represent them) and background uncorrelated parts (we
usually use
to represent them). Hence, our goal is to predict the
corresponding label map of an arbitrary medical image of size H × W ×
C. The map consists of “0" and “1,"where H denotes the height of the
image W is the width of the image and C denotes the corresponding
channel number. Please see Fig. 1 for a more intuitive understanding of
medical image segmentation.
The underlying hypothesis behind our architecture is that the model
can capture fine-grained details more efficiently when the local feature
maps extracted from the U-Net network branch are fused with the global
feature maps extracted from the ConvNeXt network branch. Comple-
mentary learning of the two branches is more conducive to improving
model segmentation performance. Moreover, following [64,65,68,70],
the two-branch model provides an efficient and complementary fusion
model. The network structure of the proposed BCU-Net is illustrated in
Fig. 2.
As illustrated in Fig. 2, the BCU-Net consists of two heterogeneous
branches. It seamlessly bridges two heterogeneous networks, ConvNeXt
and U-Net, smartly and conveniently. Traditionally, ConvNeXt is not a
U-shaped (encoder-decoder) model and is used only for image classifi-
cation and object detection. To complete medical image segmentation,
we first add a “decoder" part into the ConvNeXt branch, whereas the
original structure is regarded as the “encoder"part of this branch. Thus,
the redesigned ConvNeXt model can meet the “encoder-decoder'
structure, which is useful for medical image segmentation. Larger con-
volutional kernels in the ConvNeXt branch can acquire a relatively large
perceptual field, which contributes to the capture of global pathological
semantics in medical images. In contrast to the ConvNeXt branch, the U-
Net branch acquires a relatively small perceptual field that contributes
to the extraction of local pathological semantic information. Finally, the
final feature map of each branch was input into the MRL module to
implement deep-level feature fusion. The two heterogeneous branches
complement each other to complete medical image segmentation. Here,
we describe BCU-Net in detail as follows:
First, in the U-Net branch, we retained its original structure as much
as possible because we were eager to determine whether the corre-
sponding performance improvement of BCU-Net originated from
another ConvNeXt branch or a two-branch structure. The U-Net branch
consists of five continuous downsampling blocks, four skip connections,
and four continuous upsampling blocks. Each downsampling block (U-
Net Block) contains two stacked 3 × 3 convolutions, one batch norm
(BN) layer [71], and a rectified linear unit (ReLU) layer. Each
up-sampling block (Up-Sample-2) contained one bilinear layer, two
stacked 3 × 3 convolutions, one BN layer, and one ReLU layer. The final
feature map
is generated by the U-Net branch and is input into the
MRL module for subsequent feature fusion. The smaller convolution in
the U-Net branch makes the proposed model sufficiently capable of
capturing local pathological semantics.

for medical image segmentation. Thus, the ConvNeXt branch comprised

2.2. Two-branch segmentation model
Recently, two-branch models have been shown to play an important
role in CV. For example, Mobile-Former [42], a parallel design of
MobileNet and Transformer with a two-way bridge between them, was
proposed to implement image classification and object detection. Tan
et al. [64] proposed a two-branch parallel deep fusion network for 3D
object detection. Neven et al. [65] designed a two-branch network for
pixel-based defect segmentation and severity estimations. Bao et al. [66]
proposed a two-branch deep network for 3D point cloud classification.
Ma et al. [67] combined a multiscale matched filter and a U-net model to
extract vascular features using three channels and fused the segmenta-
tion results of the three channels.
Recently, inspired by the two-branch studies above, researchers
introduced the two-branch idea into medical image segmentation. Chen
et al. [43] utilized a bridging method to connect two U-Nets, making full
use of the complementarity of the two networks to improve the final
performance. Kumar et al. [68] proposed a dual U-Net architecture using
an improved Swish function for brain-tumor segmentation. Zhuang et al.
[69] implemented two U-Net links for retinal vessel segmentation.
Zhuang's model contains multiple encoder-decoder branches and allows
for more information flow. Huang et al. [70] designed a two-branch
U-Net model that allowed one branch to be trained using weighting
schemes, emphasizing harder examples to improve the overall seg-
mentation performance.
In summary, these two-branch methods [43,68–70] added too many
skip connections between the two networks. This increases the
complexity of the corresponding model and reduces its practicality. Each
branch of these models focuses on the extraction of local pathological
semantics. This significant global information, which is useful for
medical image segmentation, is partly ignored. Third, the class imbal-
ance problem remains a serious problem in current methods. Finally,
most of these studies tended to use homogeneous rather than hetero-
geneous networks to create two-branch segmentation models. The im-
plicit pathological correlations between heterogeneous branches are not
fully mined, which helps boost the final segmentation performance.
These problems inspired us to design a novel two-branch segmentation
model using two heterogeneous but complementary neural networks.
The new model should make the best of all types of pathological se-
mantics and address the class-imbalance problem. However, it does not
require additional parameters, which improves its practicality. Table 1
provides detailed descriptions of the aforementioned studies.
2.3. Research motivations
Inspired by Mobile-Former [42], W-net [43], and Medical Trans-
former [44], we propose a two-branch segmentation model called
BCU-Net. Our research motivation is fourfold: First, the local and global
pathological semantics should be considered. We leverage the advan-
tages of ConvNeXt for global interaction and U-Net for local processing.
Second, we investigated the possibility of bridging two heterogeneous
networks smartly and conveniently to extract sufficient complementary
pathological semantics. Third, we must bridge the two heterogeneous
branches efficiently and alleviate the class-imbalance problem. Finally,
we propose a flexible network structure to reduce the complexity of the
proposed model. Based on these motivations, we propose the BCU-Net
for medical image segmentation.

5. Conclusion
We considered improving the efficiency of the traditional U-Net
model and proposed a novel BCU-Net for medical image segmentation.
We first modified the original ConvNeXt to meet the standard “encoder-
decoder" demand. We made ConvNeXt suitable for medical-image seg-
mentation. We then seamlessly bridged the redesigned ConvNeXt and U-
Net to create BCU-Net. BCU-Net comprises two parallel but comple-
mentary network branches. One branch is ConvNeXt and the other is U-
Net. Finally, an MRL module is proposed to efficiently and smoothly
bridge the two heterogeneous branches. This module also alleviates the
class imbalance problem using recall loss and facilitates the deep-level
fusion of global and local pathological semantics originating from
different branches.
Extensive experimental results on six public datasets show that BCU-
Net is highly competitive for medical image segmentation. Moreover, it
has two-dimensional generalization capabilities. First, it is effective for
diverse datasets, including blood vessel and polyp images. Second, it
handles medical images of different resolutions well. In addition, the
ConvNeXt and U-Net branches contributed to improving the final per-
formance. An important advantage of the BCU-Net is that it is more
flexible owing to its seamless plug-and-play structure. Each branch can
be replaced with other off-the-shelf segmentation networks to further
improve the segmentation performance. Moreover, BCU-Net is easier to
reproduce and deploy, thereby promoting its practicality.
In the future, we plan to make more active interactions (diverse
“bridging" methods) between the intermediate feature layers of each
branch. We hope that this optimization will achieve excellent results in
each evaluation metric. We intend to compress BCU-Net using state-of-
the-art knowledge distillation methods [104,105]. This helps to narrow
the gap between theoretical research and practical applications. Further,
some mainstream domain adaption methods may be used to address the
“gap" between different datasets, which helps alleviate the data scarcity
issue.
